modules.title: The United Nations
modules.html:
1. Formation

The United Nations was founded on 24 October 1945 when the Charter, drafted at the San Francisco Conference, came into force, replacing the failed League of Nations. Headquarters: New York. Membership: 193 states. Nigeria joined on 7 October 1960 as the 99th member.

2. Aims

  1. Maintain international peace and security.
  2. Develop friendly relations based on equal rights and self-determination.
  3. Achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems.
  4. Promote respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms.
  5. Be a centre for harmonising the actions of nations.

3. Principal Organs

OrganCompositionFunctions
General AssemblyAll 193 members, one vote eachDeliberates on any Charter matter, approves budget, admits members, elects non-permanent SC members
Security Council15 members: 5 permanent (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) with veto, 10 elected for two yearsPrimary responsibility for peace and security; authorises sanctions and peacekeeping
Economic and Social Council54 membersCoordinates economic, social and humanitarian work and specialised agencies
Trusteeship CouncilSuspended 1994Supervised trust territories until Palau's independence
International Court of Justice15 judges, The HagueSettles disputes between states; advisory opinions
SecretariatHeaded by the Secretary-GeneralAdministration and day-to-day work

4. Specialised Agencies

WHO, UNESCO, FAO, ILO, UNICEF, UNHCR, IMF, World Bank, IAEA, UNDP, UNIDO, WTO (related).

5. Achievements and Problems

Achievements: prevention of a third world war; decolonisation of more than 80 territories; peacekeeping from the Congo to Mali; the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948); eradication of smallpox and near-eradication of polio; humanitarian relief; development goals (MDGs and SDGs); disarmament treaties.

Problems: the veto paralysing the Security Council; lack of an independent standing army; dependence on member contributions and arrears; big-power dominance and calls for reform of the Council; disregard of resolutions by powerful states; slow bureaucracy.

6. Nigeria and the UN

Nigeria has served several terms as a non-permanent member of the Security Council, chaired the Special Committee Against Apartheid, contributed over 200,000 troops to peacekeeping since the Congo in 1960, produced senior UN officials, and campaigns for an African permanent seat with veto power.

examples.q: Explain how the veto power can paralyse the Security Council.
examples.a: A substantive resolution fails if any of the five permanent members votes against it, regardless of majority support. Thus a proposal to sanction or authorise force against a P5 member or its ally is effectively impossible — as seen repeatedly over Syria, Ukraine and the Middle East. This reflects 1945 power realities, protects great-power interests and is the central argument for Security Council reform, including Africa's demand for permanent representation.

examples.q: Why does Nigeria campaign for a permanent Security Council seat?
examples.a: Africa has 54 UN members and is the subject of most Council agenda items, yet has no permanent seat or veto. Nigeria points to its population, economy, and unmatched African record of peacekeeping and peace enforcement as qualifications. A permanent seat would give Africa a voice in binding decisions affecting it and correct a structure frozen in the aftermath of 1945.

modules.title: The Commonwealth and OPEC
modules.html:
1. The Commonwealth of Nations

A voluntary association of 56 independent states, mostly former British colonies, tracing its modern form to the 1949 London Declaration. Headquarters: Marlborough House, London. The King is Head of the Commonwealth (a symbolic office); a Secretary-General heads the Secretariat.

  • Aims: promote democracy, human rights, good governance and the rule of law; foster economic and social development and trade; encourage educational, cultural and sporting cooperation; support small member states; consultation on world affairs.
  • Organs and instruments: the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), the Secretariat, the Commonwealth Foundation, Commonwealth of Learning, Commonwealth Fund for Technical Cooperation, the Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG), and the Commonwealth Games.
  • Achievements: scholarships and technical assistance; election observation; the Harare Declaration (1991) on democratic values; pressure against apartheid South Africa (which left in 1961 and returned in 1994); suspension of Nigeria (1995–1999), Pakistan, Fiji and Zimbabwe for undemocratic conduct.
  • Problems: no enforcement power beyond suspension; unequal economic weight; declining relevance to trade; funding limitations.

2. OPEC

The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries was founded at the Baghdad Conference, 14 September 1960, by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela. Headquarters moved from Geneva to Vienna in 1965. Nigeria joined in 1971.

  • Objectives: coordinate and unify petroleum policies of member states; secure fair and stable prices for producers; ensure efficient, economic and regular supply to consumers; guarantee a fair return on capital to investors; eliminate harmful and unnecessary price fluctuations.
  • Organs: the Conference of ministers (supreme organ, meets at least twice yearly), the Board of Governors, the Secretariat headed by a Secretary-General, and the Economic Commission.
  • Instruments: production quotas allocated to members, price benchmarks, and coordination with non-OPEC producers (OPEC+ since 2016).
  • Achievements: transfer of pricing power from the international oil companies to producing states in the 1970s; higher revenues funding national development; the 1973 embargo demonstrated collective bargaining power; the OPEC Fund for International Development assists poorer countries; technical training and data.
  • Problems: quota violations and cheating; political and religious rivalries among members (Iran–Saudi Arabia, Iran–Iraq war); dependence on a single commodity; competition from non-OPEC producers, US shale and renewables; global energy transition and climate pressure.

3. Nigeria's Benefits and Obligations

Through OPEC Nigeria gains price stabilisation, market intelligence, training and a share of collective bargaining power; it accepts quota discipline in return, which sometimes conflicts with domestic revenue needs. Through the Commonwealth Nigeria gains scholarships, technical cooperation and diplomatic access, and accepts scrutiny of its democratic conduct.

examples.q: Why did OPEC's 1973 action reshape world politics?
examples.a: During the Arab–Israeli war, Arab OPEC members imposed an oil embargo on states supporting Israel and cut production, quadrupling crude prices. It transferred pricing power from the multinational oil companies to producing governments, created huge petro-dollar surpluses (Nigeria's oil boom of the 1970s), triggered recession and inflation in the West, and proved that developing-country producer cartels could exert real leverage — fuelling demands for a New International Economic Order.

examples.q: Evaluate the effect of Nigeria's suspension from the Commonwealth in 1995.
examples.a: Following the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight Ogoni activists during the Auckland CHOGM, Nigeria was suspended for breaching the Harare Declaration. The effect was largely diplomatic and reputational: loss of technical assistance and observer status, deepened isolation of the Abacha regime, and encouragement for internal pro-democracy forces. It did not force immediate change — showing the Commonwealth's reliance on moral rather than coercive pressure — but Nigeria's readmission in 1999 was tied to the return of civil rule.

quiz.q: The United Nations was founded on:
quiz.solution: The Charter came into force on 24 October 1945, celebrated as UN Day.

quiz.q: The UN organ with primary responsibility for peace and security is the:
quiz.solution: The Security Council may authorise sanctions and the use of force.

quiz.q: How many permanent members does the Security Council have?
quiz.solution: The USA, UK, France, Russia and China hold permanent seats with veto power.

quiz.q: The International Court of Justice sits at:
quiz.solution: The ICJ is located in the Peace Palace, The Hague.

quiz.q: Nigeria joined the United Nations in:
The Trusteeship Council suspended operations in:
quiz.solution: It suspended work after Palau, the last trust territory, became independent in 1994.
The Baghdad Conference of September 1960 created OPEC.
Nigeria became a member in 1971 after oil exports grew.
The Secretariat moved from Geneva to Vienna in 1965.

quiz.q: The supreme organ of OPEC is the:
quiz.solution: The Conference of member-state ministers determines policy.

quiz.q: The Commonwealth declaration on democratic values adopted in 1991 was the:
quiz.solution: The Harare Declaration committed members to democracy and human rights.

quiz.q: Nigeria was suspended from the Commonwealth in:
quiz.solution: Suspension followed the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa in November 1995.

quiz.q: The Commonwealth body that deals with serious violations of political values is:
quiz.solution: The Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group handles persistent violations.

quiz.q: Which is a UN specialised agency?
quiz.solution: The World Health Organization is a UN specialised agency.

quiz.q: A major weakness of the UN is:
options: Use of the veto by permanent members
quiz.solution: The veto can block action even where the majority supports it.
Members agree output ceilings to influence global supply and price.
